Package io.thymekit

@NullMarked package io.thymekit
thymekit — domain-agnostic interface elements.

Every element is a triple: a Java API (this package), a Thymeleaf fragment served from the jar, and a CSS file whose appearance is tuned by the consumer through --tk-* custom properties.

The canon

  • An element owns its concept. If a concept has an element — heading, caption, section — everything that needs it composes that element instead of writing its own markup. A new element is therefore always followed by a pass over the existing ones.
  • Shape: factory(core) → options → build() yields Element, the single currency of composition. Wide points accept Element<?>, narrow points name the marker; where the marker is erased, Element.requireAdapter(io.thymekit.Element<?>, java.lang.String, java.lang.String) guards at runtime.
  • One dispatcher. Everything renders through thymekit/element: render(e) for one element, renderAll(items) for a flow, slot(e, name) for a slot, scripts(items) for behaviour scripts. Containers know no list of bricks.
  • The adapter name is the contract version. Changing the meaning of a descriptor key means a new adapter (<name>ElV2), not a new key in the old one.
  • Guards live in the builder: null with the argument's name, invalid state on build.

Elements of the core

The core holds domain-empty bricks a page rests on. The rest of the kit's elements live one layer below for now and come back one at a time: an element stays in the core not because it happens to be here, but after it has been reviewed on the showcase.

  • Heading — owner of headings: h1(text)…h6(text) with an anchor id, a link (href plus Rel values and newTab), the language of the text and screen-reader-only. No default level: it decides the outline, so the author states it. The outline of a page they make is checked by Outline.
  • Caption — owner of captions in four roles (eyebrow, subtitle, label, meta): short text attached to something, never a heading and never a form label. A caption may carry a machine-readable time and a lang of its own.
  • Hero — the header of the page: a heading group, an optional badge and an optional action row; its core is the H1 alone, and the rule under the group is drawn by CSS.
  • Md — the text of a page: markdown rendered by the #md dialect and sanitised, or an empty state with an affordance beside it. linkRel says what the links of somebody else's text are. Content, not structure — a heading around it belongs to Section.
  • Section — a titled part of a page: a heading and a slot for whatever goes under it. Anything needing a titled area composes this instead of writing its own <section>.
  • PageModel — the page canvas. It builds two elements: the page itself, which draws the <main> landmark with the flow inside it, and the head of the document (title, description, canonical, image, PageModel.Robots). Both go through the same dispatcher as everything else, so composition is closed at the top as well as at the bottom. render() uses the default document, render(view) one of your own.
  • Outline — the headings of a page, and whether they add up to something a reader can walk. Checked by the canvas before rendering; it lives apart from the currency because an outline is a property of a page, and because knowing what a heading is belongs to the element that owns headings.
  • Anchors — the addresses inside a page, and whether two things answer to one of them. Counts the anchors the kit puts down, not every key called id: what that word means in an element of yours is yours to say.
  • Rel — what a link says about itself, and the policy that goes with it: the guards and the order of the values, the noopener a new tab cannot lose, and the attribute they are written as. Public, so an element of yours links exactly as the kit's do.
  • ElementContract — the walk over a triple: the kit checks its own elements with it, and hands the same walk to whoever writes one.
  • Composable — whatever becomes an element: every builder here, and Element itself. A place that takes an element takes this, so nothing has to be written between one element and the next.
  • Element.raw(template, fragment) wraps a consumer fragment as an element, Element.script(...) a behaviour script, and Element.Descriptor.of(...) is how a consumer mints an element of its own.
